findings.summary: TwinSnapshot FactIDs for stale facts are appended in the non-deterministic input order of facts, causing unstable snapshot identities.
evidence: In BuildTwinSnapshot, stale facts are appended to the stale slice as they are encountered in the unsorted facts input.
The stale slice is then iterated to populate field.FactIDs without sorting, unlike the matching slice which is explicitly sorted.
Because twinSnapshotID hashes the JSON representation of these fields, different input orders of the same facts produce different snapshot IDs.

findings.summary: Token usage sum can silently overflow int64 to exactly zero, incorrectly rejecting valid non-empty evaluator runs.
evidence: validateEvaluatorRun sums InputTokens, OutputTokens, CacheReadTokens, and CacheWriteTokens using int64 addition.
If the sum overflows to exactly 0 (e.g., each field is 1<<62), the validation fails with 'requires non-negative, non-empty measured token usage'.
Unlike cost calculations in scheduler.go and value.go, this sum lacks an overflow check against math.MaxInt64.

findings.summary: EvaluatorMetric.FalsePositiveRate computes the False Discovery Rate (FP / (TP + FP)) rather than the statistical False Positive Rate.
evidence: MeasureEvaluatorBatch calculates FalsePositiveRate as metric.FalsePositives / metric.DisposedFindings.
DisposedFindings is the sum of VerifiedDefects (TP) and FalsePositives (FP).
The ratio FP / (TP + FP) is the False Discovery Rate, whereas False Positive Rate is strictly FP / Actual Negatives.

findings.summary: Absolute tolerance of 1e-9 fails to absorb float64 rounding errors for large demands or capacities, breaking max-flow feasibility checks.
evidence: The feasible function checks g.max(source, sink)+tolerance < total using a hardcoded absolute tolerance of 1e-9.
WorkItem.Demand and Resource.Capacity are only bounded by being finite and positive.
For large values (e.g., 1e15), float64 precision gaps far exceed 1e-9, causing valid max-flows to be rejected due to normal floating-point rounding.

findings.summary: Alternative-inventory change detection compares `fmt.Sprint(ids)` where ids is a sorted []string; because fmt.Sprint is not injective (e.g. ["a","b"] and ["a b"] both render as "[a b]"), two scenarios with genuinely different alternative identities can be treated as identical, silently bypassing the inventory-change guard the doc promises.
evidence: value_scenario.go builds `encodedIDs := fmt.Sprint(ids)` and compares strings; an executable probe (scenario1 alternatives ["a","b"], scenario2 ["a b"]) returned nil error, confirming the guard was bypassed
go test ./internal/optimization with a probe constructing colliding ID sets shows AssessValueScenarios does not reject the identity change

findings.summary: Policy selection-change detection uses `fmt.Sprint(policyResult.Selected)` as the comparison key; the same non-injective rendering means two different Selected sets can compare equal when an alternative ID contains a space, so SelectionChanges can be falsely reported as false.
evidence: value_policy.go sets `selection := fmt.Sprint(policyResult.Selected)` and compares to firstSelection; fmt.Sprint on []string is not injective for space-bearing IDs
same root cause as value_scenario.go; a crafted ID set renders distinct selections identically

findings.summary: BuildTwinSnapshot detects conflicting facts by comparing `string(fact.Value) != string(field.Value)` (raw bytes after json.Compact, which preserves key order), so two semantically identical JSON values with different key order are reported as CONFLICTING rather than KNOWN.
evidence: probe: two facts with values {"x":1,"y":2} and {"y":2,"x":1} for the same requirement produced Status CONFLICTING, though the values are semantically equal
json.Compact in NewTemporalFact does not canonicalize object key order, so conflict detection is byte-order sensitive

findings.summary: NewTemporalFact derives the content-addressed fact ID from the marshaled struct including the byte-exact Value, so semantically equal facts with different JSON key order yield different fact IDs, fragmenting identity for identical observations.
evidence: probe: NewTemporalFact on the same logical value with keys in two orders produced id1 != id2
fact identity is byte-sensitive, not value-canonical (no JCS/canonical JSON normalization of Value)

findings.summary: When a Problem supplies a CostModel but no item carries EstimatedCostMicros (hasCosts==false), validate() skips CostModel currency/source/asOf checks entirely, so a malformed CostModel (bad currency, empty source, non-RFC3339 asOf) is accepted and echoed into Result.CostModel.
evidence: validate() only enforces CostModel fields inside `if hasCosts {...}`; a probe with CostModel{Currency:"bad",Source:"",AsOf:"not-a-time"} and costless items returned err=nil and the malformed CostModel in the Result
the Result then carries an unvalidated cost model that downstream cost-evidence checks (MeasureCostAccuracy) never re-validate for well-formedness

findings.summary: On an exact load tie with optimizeCost enabled, a candidate with a KNOWN cost is preferred over one whose cost is UNKNOWN (`cheaper := optimizeCost && candidateKnown && (!bestKnown || ...)`), so a missing estimate is effectively treated as worst-case for placement even though the doc states only that a missing estimate 'suppresses aggregate cost' and is 'not treated as free'; the tie-break direction is undocumented.
evidence: round() sets cheaper true when candidateKnown && !bestKnown; a probe with one known-cost and one unknown-cost equal-capacity resource assigned the item to the known-cost resource on the tie
ADVISORY-OPTIMIZATION.md says 'a missing estimate remains unknown and suppresses aggregate cost instead of being treated as free' but does not state that unknown cost loses ties to any known cost

findings.summary: The binding between an EvaluatorRun and the immutable git snapshot is only format-checked: validateEvaluatorRun requires InputSnapshotID to match `snap_`+64-hex, but no code recomputes the platform/ archive digest or cross-checks it against a receipt produced by build-evaluator-snapshot.sh, so a run can claim any well-formed snap_ ID that does not correspond to the audited commit.
evidence: validateEvaluatorRun calls only validContentID(run.InputSnapshotID, "snap_") (length/prefix/hex), never hashing the tree or comparing to build-evaluator-snapshot.sh output

build-evaluator-snapshot.sh emits snap_<sha256-of-tar>, but there is no executable gate linking a recorded EvaluatorRun.InputSnapshotID to that receipt; git grep shows InputSnapshotID is only ever format-validated

findings.summary: AssessDORA computes windowDuration = windowEnd.Sub(windowStart) and later uses windowDuration.Nanoseconds() as a big.Rat denominator and WindowSeconds; for windows approaching/exceeding the int64 duration range (~292 years) time.Time.Sub saturates and Nanoseconds() can overflow, so WindowSeconds/DeploymentFrequencyPerSecond silently misreport for extreme windows with no guard.
evidence: dora.go: `windowDuration := windowEnd.Sub(windowStart)`, `exactDurationSeconds(windowDuration)`, and `SetFrac(..., big.NewInt(windowDuration.Nanoseconds()))` use the saturated int64 nanosecond count
a probe at 290 years produced a finite WindowSeconds (9145440000) with no error; there is no upper-bound check on the window such as exists for MaximumDurationSec in experiment plans
